SMTO-ART-0028 — SMTO's scheduled cleanup of old Task files didn't finish

GUID: 616b0410-68a8-4b21-b567-6acc33d3dd87
Slug: artifact-cleanup-failed
Domain: ART · Subsystem: art

What happened

  • SMTO removes old Task files on a schedule, and its last cleanup didn't finish. Some expired files may still be using disk space. Files you're keeping aren't affected, and SMTO tries again in about an hour.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. After about an hour, open Artifacts from this run on any Task and read the Last cleanup line under the retention setting. That line shows when the most recent cleanup ran and whether it ended with an error.
  2. If the computer running SMTO is low on disk space, tell the person who manages SMTO now instead of deleting files yourself. While cleanup keeps failing, expired files build up, and the cause is on the server, such as a folder SMTO can't read or write.
  3. Don't delete files from SMTO's data folder by hand to free space. Cleanup skips files that running, scheduled or linked Tasks still need; deleting by hand skips those checks and can break those Tasks.

What success looks like

  • The Last cleanup line shows a recent time with no error after it.

If it still fails

  • If the Last cleanup line still shows an error after a few hours, select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO, mentioning any disk-space warnings. Don't remove Task file folders by hand.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • The artifact MaintenanceWorker's scheduled run_once pass raised an exception; the worker logged it, recorded a safe error in artifact_maintenance, and will retry on its next hourly pass.

What this means

  • The maintenance worker catches a scheduled run_once exception, records a safe failure where possible and returns to its existing hourly wait loop. Artifact publication and presentation remain separate from the command that produced a file. Only an explicit pre-dispatch rejection proves that new command did not run; diagnostics do not collect, transfer, quarantine or delete files.

Why this can happen

  • The maintenance worker catches a scheduled run_once exception, records a safe failure where possible and returns to its existing hourly wait loop.

How to diagnose it

  • Inspect the maintenance log and ownership/storage condition without deleting protected files manually.

How to fix it

  • Find "Artifact maintenance failed; next hourly pass will retry" and its stack trace in the Server log, then fix the cause (for example artifact-store directory permissions, free disk space or state-store errors) and let the next scheduled pass run. Do not delete live, scheduled or referenced artifacts, or weaken the protection checks, to make cleanup succeed.
  • Inspect the maintenance log and artifact-store access. Preserve live or referenced artifacts; do not delete them to bypass maintenance ownership checks.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • The worker's later supported pass completes while live/referenced artifacts stay protected.

What not to do

  • Do not remove retained state or weaken trust checks to make an unavailable dependency appear healthy.

Technical notes

  • Artifact publication and presentation remain separate from the command that produced a file. Only an explicit pre-dispatch rejection proves that new command did not run; diagnostics do not collect, transfer, quarantine or delete files.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
